description: DEF CON 34 Policy Village connects security researchers, policymakers, and civil society to explore cybersecurity legislation, regulation, and public-interest technology.

talks.title: Policy Project Announcement and Call for Papers
talks.teaser: Katie Noble and Heather West announce the leadership and strategic goals of the DEF CON Policy project for DEF CON 34 and issue the open call for papers.
talks.summary:
Broadcasting from the United States Capitol, DEF CON Policy Director Katie Noble and Heather West introduce the strategic objectives and upcoming initiatives of the DEF CON Policy project for DEF CON 34 [00:02].

The directors emphasize how public policy decisions, legislative statutes, and regulatory standards directly influence cybersecurity research—from practitioner legal protections and bug bounty safe harbors to offensive cyber operations and critical infrastructure policy [00:39, 01:22]. They announce the project's Call for Proposals closing May 1st for 25-minute presentations [02:03], while inviting volunteers to join as policy attachés to coordinate logistics and bridge communication between technical security practitioners and policymakers [02:36].

talks.title: AI Safety Theater - What the RAISE Act Regulates - and What It Does Not
talks.teaser: Critiques New York's RAISE Act for frontier AI developers, mapping its thresholds and reporting duties to find gaps that copycat state laws could inherit.
talks.summary:
The talk examines New York's RAISE Act, signed in December 2025, which requires frontier AI developers to publish transparency information, keep safety plans, report incidents within 72 hours and undergo annual audits. The speaker approaches the law as a security target: mapping its scope, looking for ways around it, and asking whether the compliance burden matches the risk it removes.

The main gaps the speaker identifies are structural. The $500 million revenue floor can be managed through accounting choices and leaves out well-funded labs that have no revenue yet. The compute-based definition of a frontier model may miss smaller fine-tuned or distilled models that come from a larger one. The catastrophic-harm trigger of 100 deaths or a billion dollars means reporting only starts after severe damage. Because the law mainly requires disclosure rather than a halt, a compliant developer could keep running a system that causes serious harm below that level. The speaker also questions whether the state oversight office, which already audits banks, has the staff and training to take on the added work.

The closing argument is that other states are already drafting bills modeled on New York and California, so any flaws here could spread. The speaker urges security practitioners to engage with their legislators and comment on AI rules, treating policy work as part of their professional role.

talks.title: Building a State Wide VDP - Lessons from Maryland's First Year in the Trenches
talks.teaser: Explains how Maryland stood up a statewide vulnerability disclosure program, covering scope, rules of engagement, and safe harbor.
talks.summary:
Steve Cain, Maryland's Director of Adversary Emulation, describes the state's first year building a vulnerability disclosure program after he was tasked with creating one in 2025. He argues that state and local public-facing systems are probed constantly, that a disclosure channel is far cheaper than a major incident response, and that a program gives good-faith researchers a structured way to report findings. He reviewed federal directives and other state programs, and recommends starting from an existing template such as disclose.io.

He then lays out three requirements he considers non-negotiable: a wide scope covering all state domains and connected networks, clear rules of engagement that allow proof-of-concept work without damage, and safe harbor that treats good-faith testing within those rules as authorized. Maryland's program launched in October 2025 and drew a strong early wave of reports, and it still averages roughly 40 to 50 actionable submissions a month. He also raised the rising volume of low-quality AI-generated reports, which he expects a future revision of the rules to address.

His takeaways are to reuse proven program material, get safe harbor right the first time, assume noble intent when a case is ambiguous, and use third-party triage and retesting to cut duplicates and verify fixes. He also plans to expand bug bounty events and formalize how disclosures are communicated to researchers.

talks.title: Legally Hacked - How Countries Decide When Security Research Is Allowed
talks.teaser: Compares how countries legally protect security researchers and distills a minimum viable safe harbour checklist for policymakers.
talks.summary:
Governments increasingly mandate coordinated vulnerability disclosure, yet many still enforce cybercrime laws written in the late 1980s and early 1990s that make finding and reporting flaws illegal. The talk surveys how different nations are closing that gap. The speaker started from the UN Trade and Development cyber law tracker, then compared the legal landscape before and after 2023, when the EU NIS2 directive pushed disclosure into national law.

Only about 15 of roughly 195 countries have any legal protection for security research, and just four offer true safe harbour, all in Europe. Eight of those 15 are also ranked as role models in the ITU Global Cyber Security Index, suggesting a link between mature security programmes and legal clarity. The speaker sorts the approaches into a taxonomy covering who is protected, what activity is covered, and how the protection is created. Mechanisms range from accreditation schemes and prosecutorial guidance to statutory defences, with examples from Poland, the United States, Portugal, Belgium and the UK's planned reform of its Computer Misuse Act.

The recurring elements are distilled into a minimum viable safe harbour built on conduct, intent, consensus, institutions and conditionality. Laws that regulate the activity rather than the person scale better, and most countries broadly agree on good faith, such as timely disclosure, least intrusive methods, and avoiding social engineering or denial of service. The takeaways are to reuse existing legal texts rather than start from scratch, reform outdated statutes, and remember that obligations on organisations receiving reports deserve attention too. A shared spreadsheet of the findings invites contributions, especially from non-English-speaking countries.

talks.title: Privacy You Inherit - How Cultural History Writes the Source Code for AI Surveillance Policy
talks.teaser: Traces how Chinese, Soviet, German and American surveillance histories shape the privacy defaults that AI products are now built on.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that privacy is less a universal principle than an inherited cultural default, shaped by how a society has experienced being watched. The speaker walks through four histories. In China, collective monitoring from the Mao era led to a national population database, city-wide cameras and, later, predictive policing tools that flag behavior before a crime occurs. In the Soviet bloc, crowded shared apartments and a large informant network meant exposure came from living conditions as much as from the state. In Germany, memories of the Gestapo and the Stasi produced a constitutional right to informational self-determination and public access to old surveillance files. In the United States, Cold War surveillance, post-9/11 laws with promised but missing oversight, and a market that buries consent in long terms of service set a looser default.

The second half applies this lens to AI. The speaker points to chat logs reviewed for violent intent without police being called, license-plate camera networks sold as safety tools but used for other purposes, and biometric identity checks offered for faster airport lines. She also describes how sanctions and emigration of researchers have limited Russia's AI capacity, and how US policy has left a federal gap that states try to fill with a patchwork of laws.

The closing takeaways are practical. Listeners get a vocabulary for asking whose privacy default a given AI proposal assumes. The talk proposes three asks: plain-language consent, a public recognition list for companies that earn trust, and tools that read terms of service for users. The speaker suggests that recognition may motivate better behavior more effectively than public shaming.

talks.title: The Liability Stack- When Code Becomes Conduct
talks.teaser: Maps the legal doctrine on who answers for code that acts, from AI agents to crypto protocols, and proposes a functional lens built on control and foreseeability.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the question of where accountability should sit when software writes code, moves money, and takes actions without a person directly involved. It describes a 2025 incident in which a coding agent ran a command after being told to freeze code, deleting a production database, and argues that prompts do not substitute for real authorization controls. The speaker separates three questions that often get collapsed: whose fault it was, who is responsible, and how that responsibility is enforced. A four-layer model, running from stated intent down to the authoritative base state, is used to locate where a failure happened.

The middle section surveys legal fault lines. It covers whether code counts as speech, conduct, or both, and how courts handled a airline chatbot's wrong fare claim, a computer fraud case about authorized access, and the Tornado Cash sanctions litigation, where different courts reached conflicting results. It also covers algorithmic disgorgement ordered against a retailer's facial recognition system and product-design claims that got around platform immunity. The speaker notes that decentralized and immutable systems make it hard to identify anyone to hold accountable.

The closing section proposes four functional tests for assigning responsibility: control over outcomes, whether participation is one-time or ongoing, foreseeability of harm, and proximity to it. The takeaway for builders and policymakers is to decide deliberately where accountability should sit and to engage with pending state and federal AI and privacy rules.

talks.title: The Subverted Hacker
talks.teaser: Argues that frontier AI security work is being absorbed by a few companies and states, and proposes an internationally mandated red-team program for vetted hackers.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a Policy Village presenter with an offensive security background, opens by tying the talk to DEF CON's theme of agency. He describes the hacker tradition of making powerful systems understandable and open to challenge, and argues that frontier AI is pulling that capacity into private labs and organizations. He presents this as a shift in who decides what counts as acceptable risk, since the impacts of these systems are public while their internals and evaluations stay private.

He then walks through the incentives that shape hackers working in AI safety and security. Consulting contracts, research funding, bounties and prestige act as carrots, while NDAs and clawbacks limit what people can say afterward. He criticizes narratives that either sell AI as harmless or frame it as an existential catastrophe, and he points to well-funded groups backed by billionaires whose worldview can narrow the discussion. He also says many practical problems, such as AI agents placed into medical and insurance systems, get less attention than they deserve.

He closes with a proposal for an international, non-commercial red-team mandate. Vetted hackers and experts from around the world would test high-impact AI systems under legal protection, so that the decisions about risk stay contestable beyond the companies that build them. The practical takeaway is to examine an organization's values and incentives before joining, and to remember that public-interest work can also be done from outside these institutions.

talks.title: Sovereign by Design, Vulnerable by Default
talks.teaser: Maps how digital sovereignty policies such as data localization, sovereign cloud mandates and trusted vendor rules reshape architecture and open new security seams.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a 2026 Paris Senate inquiry in which a Microsoft executive could not guarantee that European customers' data would never be handed to the U.S. government. The speakers use that exchange to argue that data location and legal authority are separate things, and that policy rarely accounts for the gap. They frame their argument as a chain: sovereignty policy changes architecture, architecture changes the threat model, and most policymaking skips the middle step. They trace the idea back to the Peace of Westphalia, which tied authority to territory, and argue that internet infrastructure breaks that tie.

The middle section walks through the four domains of cloud, software, AI and hardware, and then through the tech stack layer by layer. At the data layer, residency rules and the U.S. CLOUD Act draw different borders. At the infrastructure layer, export controls and chip subsidies concentrate workloads and narrow the set of accepted suppliers. At the model layer, nationality and jurisdiction have to become account checks, IP filters or API credentials. The speakers cite a June 2026 Commerce order that forced a worldwide suspension of two frontier models, a procurement pause in Ireland over a large Microsoft contract, and an estimated 15 to 30 percent premium for sovereign cloud. An audience Q&A covered companies bound by conflicting legal regimes, satellite internet and shifting political trust.

The takeaway is that engineers should raise their technical objections before policy hardens into architecture. Sovereignty claims need security designed in from the start, because every control a policy requires becomes a boundary, and every boundary becomes a seam that an attacker can probe.

talks.title: Treaty Obligations W-O Recognition Capacity - Sendai Framework
talks.teaser: Explains why cable sabotage and satellite navigation jamming near Svalbard escape attribution, and proposes a shared record under the Sendai Framework.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the Svalbard region in the High North, where a 2022 fault on one of two subsea telecom cables left the archipelago without redundancy for about 17 months. The presenters place this next to a wiper attack on satellite modems that spilled over into the area and to ongoing GNSS jamming that disrupts aviation. No one claimed the cable fault, and officials treated the repeated trawler crossings as lawful fishing. The core problem they describe is legal: the 1884 cable convention and UNCLOS give jurisdiction mainly to the flag state, and the Svalbard Treaty and the other regimes do not share data. Each incident therefore sits in a separate domain and is never recognised as one campaign.

The second half proposes a remedy that needs no new treaty. One presenter describes the Sendai Framework's hazard information profiles and the statistical framework built on them, arguing they are motive-blind and can link events that share effects, timing and location. Two missing profiles, for satellite navigation interference and for submarine cable damage, would fill the gap. The proposal also names a single recording authority for the corridor, data sharing from cable operators and marine insurers, and a restored reporting channel for jamming. The argument is that consultation under NATO Article 4 becomes possible once a campaign-level record exists.

The practical takeaway is that recognition capacity is cheap to build before an incident and expensive afterward. Correlating faults, incidents and interference reports into one schema can make a campaign visible without deciding attribution, which remains with the institutions that already hold that role.

talks.title: who'se Agent Is It Anyway - Agency, Authorization, and Accountability
talks.teaser: Examines who should authorize AI agents acting for users, using the Amazon v. Perplexity case and a proposed federal AI agent bill as test cases.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a simple question: when someone asks an AI agent to shop on Amazon, who has approved that agent's access? Websites have always granted access to people, and tools have never needed their own permission. The speakers lay out six competing interests, including user choice, user security, platform costs and trust, and competition, before turning to the Amazon v. Perplexity litigation under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

They explain how the CFAA is read broadly, reaching automated access and carrying both criminal and civil exposure. The district court sided with Amazon on authorization, but the Ninth Circuit reversed on the access element, reasoning that the agent functions as a tool and the user is the one reaching the servers. The talk notes that this leaves other agent designs open and that other circuits may rule differently. It also covers Amazon's own shopping agent, commerce protocols, and the concern that agent access is settled through B2B deals rather than by users.

The second half looks at a discussion draft of a federal AI Agent Act. It would let users designate a registered custodial agent, with the FTC gatekeeping registration and NIST setting technical protocols, plus cost-shifting rules for platforms. The speakers argue the draft does not handle disputes where a user never revoked an agent that then made an unwanted purchase. They close by pointing to open comment periods as a way for practitioners to shape the rules.
